title: Convenio de Hostelería de A Coruña 2025
summary: Conoce las novedades del Convenio de Hostelería de Coruña para 2025: ajustes salariales, regulación de horas extras, descansos, vacaciones y derechos laborales.
body_text: Sabemos que llevar un restaurante ya es un trabajo intenso como para, además, descifrar normativas laborales con lenguaje enrevesado. Por eso, aquí te contamos, sin rodeos, lo esencial sobre el Convenio Colectivo de Hostelería de la Provincia de A Coruña, vigente hasta finales de 2024. Este convenio marca las reglas del juego entre empresas y trabajadores del sector hostelero en la provincia. Tenerlo bien controlado te ayuda a anticiparte a problemas legales, gestionar mejor a tu equipo y ganar en estabilidad operativa. Puntos clave que debes tener en el radar Vigencia : Desde el 1 de enero de 2019 hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2024. Subidas salariales pactadas: 4% en 2022, 3,75% en 2023 y 4% en 2024. Revisión en 2025: Si el IPC acumulado entre 2022 y 2024 supera el 11,75%, se aplicará una subida adicional del 50% sobre la diferencia. Jornada anual máxima: 1.792 horas de trabajo efectivo. ¿A qué negocios afecta este convenio? A todos los que operan en el sector hostelero dentro de la provincia de A Coruña. Esto incluye desde hoteles y bares hasta discotecas, restaurantes o cafeterías. Fue publicado en el BOP en diciembre de 2022 y sirve como base legal para relaciones laborales equilibradas. Aspectos generales que regula el convenio Jornada laboral: El límite anual es de 1.792 horas , con una distribución semanal promedio de 40 horas. En cuanto al descanso, se establecen 1,5 días ininterrumpidos si la jornada es continuada, o 2 si es partida. Salarios: Durante la vigencia del convenio, los salarios han aumentado gradualmente: 4% en 2022, 3,75% en 2023 y otro 4% en 2024. En caso de que el IPC acumulado entre 2022 y 2024 supere el 11,75%, se actualizarán las tablas salariales en 2025 aplicando el 50% de esa diferencia. Extras y complementos que conviene tener presentes Pagas extraordinarias : Tres al año (julio, septiembre y diciembre), calculadas sobre el salario garantizado más complementos por antigüedad, manutención y alojamiento si aplican. Pueden prorratearse. Plus de nocturnidad : Un 1% extra por trabajar entre las 22:00 y 00:00 h, y un 25% si es entre las 00:00 y 06:00 h, salvo que ya esté incluido en el salario base. Horas extra : Se pagan con un 25% adicional o se pueden compensar con 1h15 de descanso por cada hora trabajada, a disfrutar en un máximo de 4 meses. Servicios extraordinarios : El convenio define tarifas para personal externo en eventos, como servicios de montaje o restaurante, actualizadas cada año. Complementos "ad personam" : Se mantienen los derechos consolidados antes de 1999, como antigüedad o quebranto de moneda, y se actualizan por IPC. Permisos retribuidos y conciliación laboral Este convenio también piensa en la vida personal. Algunos ejemplos de permisos: Matrimonio : 16 días naturales. Nacimiento, adopción o acogida: 4 días. Hospitalización o fallecimiento de familiares hasta 2º grado: 4 días. Visitas médicas de hijos menores de 12: hasta 12 horas/año con justificante. Mudanza: 1 día (más si es fuera de la provincia). Lactancia : 1 hora diaria o acumulación en 15 días. Exámenes prenatales y preparación al parto: justificables. Contratación, temporalidad y fijos-discontinuos: lo que debes saber 65% de plantilla fija : Las empresas con actividad estable deben tener al menos un 65% de trabajadores indefinidos. Conversión de temporales : Contratos formativos o de duración determinada pueden pasar a indefinidos según la ley. Fijos-discontinuos : Mínimo de 5 meses de trabajo al año. Preaviso de 10 días para reincorporación. Jornada mínima: 4h/día o 20h/semana. Si se superan los 5 meses de media en dos años, se consolida el 50% del extra trabajado. Cada empresa debe tener un censo actualizado de este personal. Preguntas Frecuentes ¿Cuál es la vigencia del actual convenio de hostelería de A Coruña? El convenio tiene una vigencia de seis años, desde el 1 de enero de 2019 hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2024. ¿Qué pasa si el convenio expira y no hay uno nuevo? El convenio continuará aplicándose en su totalidad hasta que se negocie y entre en vigor uno nuevo. ¿Qué antigüedad se reconoce? A partir del 1 de enero de 1999, no se generan nuevos derechos por antigüedad. Sin embargo, quienes ya hubiesen consolidado alguna cantidad antes de esa fecha, la mantendrán como un complemento “ad personam” que se actualizará anualmente según el IPC ¿Cuántos días de vacaciones me corresponden? El convenio establece un mínimo de 30 días naturales de vacaciones anuales, que pueden disfrutarse de forma continuada o fraccionada en periodos mínimos de 7 días. ¿Cómo se pagan las horas extra? Las horas extra se retribuyen con un incremento del 25% sobre la hora ordinaria o, alternativamente, pueden compensarse con 1 hora y 15 minutos de descanso por cada hora trabajada. title: Measuring Agentic Complexity
summary: Learn eight practical lenses, from task surface to explainability, that let you chart, score, and tame agentic complexity before it bites back.
body_text: Picture a street magician spinning plates, juggling flaming torches, and telling jokes to a restless crowd—all while balancing on a slack-line. That’s more or less the daily life of a modern AI agent. It must keep track of everything you’ve ever asked it, sniff out the right data source, choose the correct tool, write a polite email, schedule a follow-up, and then remember to nudge you about sunscreen before the weekend. The question isn’t “Can the agent do a trick?” —it’s “How many flaming torches can we toss in before the whole act wobbles?” In other words: how do we measure an agent’s complexity before it turns into a beautiful, un-debuggable mess? Below is a framework I’ve found useful. Think of it as eight camera angles on the same performance. Each lens tells you something different about the risk, capability, and maintainability of an agentic system . Stack them together and you get a surprisingly crisp portrait of just how hairy things are about to become. 1. Task Surface – What’s on the Plate? The first thing to count is the surface area of the agent’s mission. A calendar bot that only schedules meetings lives on a postage stamp. A “personal COO” that handles flights, invoices, legal redlines, and relationship counselling sprawls across a dinner table. Complexity rises whenever tasks are both numerous and inter-dependent : your fundraising assistant can’t draft a perfect email until the research agent has pulled donor history, which itself depends on the CRM-sync agent having cleaned last night’s import. Mapping those dependency chains is the fastest way to spot hidden cliffs. 2. Context Bandwidth – How Much World Does It See? Give an agent a 32-k-token window, no external memory, and it’s basically near-sighted. Bolt on a knowledge graph, long-term vector store, live news feeds, and sensor data, and you’ve created an information firehose. The wider the Context Bandwidth , the more variables every downstream decision must juggle. Back-of-the-napkin metric: “effective working memory” —tokens plus any external look-ups the agent can perform in one reasoning pass. Double that number and you’ve more than doubled your cognitive chaos. 3. Decision Autonomy – How Often Does It Phone Home? Autonomy isn’t a switch; it’s a dimmer. A safe, obedient bot drafts one email, then sheepishly asks you to click “Send.” A rogue-ish planner slams through a three-week donation cadence and only pings you at the end with a victory dance. The fewer hand-offs to a human, the more latent branches you must trust the agent to navigate solo —each with its own failure modes and ethical minefields. Track “human touchpoints per workflow” and watch that figure like you would watch a toddler near a swimming pool. 4. Tool Entropy – How Many APIs Are in the Orchestra? Every tool integration is a fresh source of power and a fresh place to catch fire. More interestingly, the order and parallelism in which those tools can be composed multiplies your state-space. A single-threaded “call GPT → call Stripe” flow is tame. An agent that conditionally fans out to Twilio, Gmail, and Vertex and then recombines the results is living in N-body-physics land. Rough rule: branching factor × number of tools = integration entropy . Keep a lid on it or invest in serious observability. 5. Temporal Depth – How Far Ahead Does It Plot? Reactive agents think in seconds; planning agents think in days; strategic agents keep a Kanban board for your entire quarter. Each extra timestep the agent reasons over multiplies the tree of possible futures it must model. You can approximate Temporal Depth by measuring the average length of a committed plan before re-planning . Agents that confidently lock a schedule for next month are an order of magnitude gnarlier than those who just answer “What’s for lunch?” 6. Interaction Topology – Lone Wolf or Wolf Pack? One agent is a point, two agents with a queue are an edge, ten specialised agents with a shared blackboard are a graph. The diameter, density, and hierarchy of that graph dictate how many emergent behaviors you’re going to see. A good sanity check: try drawing the message-passing diagram on a single sheet of paper. If you run out of space, congratulations—your complexity just grew faster than your whiteboard. 7. Adaptation Rate – How Fast Can It Rewrite Itself? We love agents that learn on the fly—right up until they do something “creative” in production. Adaptation Rate is about policy churn per unit time . Fine-tuning nightly? Swapping reasoning chains based on live A/Bs? Cool, but be prepared for yesterday’s logs to be useless when today’s incident hits. Guardrails, evaluation suites, and rollback levers become non-negotiable once the agent can mutate faster than your engineers can finish lunch. 8. Explainability Gradient – Can We Still Follow the Thread? Paradoxically, the more powerful an agent becomes, the hazier its motives look. If you can no longer produce a simple causal trace (“Email B exists because Fact A plus Rule C”), you’re operating on a steep Explainability Gradient. Low gradients are comfy; high gradients are where surprises—and compliance officers—live. One quick proxy: “minutes for a human to audit a decision.” When that number goes from five to fifty, complexity has sprinted ahead of transparency. Turning Lenses into Numbers You don’t need a PhD to start charting this. A simple 1-to-5 score on each lens is enough to sketch a complexity radar for your system. Do it at every major release: Baseline today’s score. Highlight spikes —a big jump on Tool Entropy with no matching bump in logging is a danger sign. Allocate budget —each extra point on a lens costs time, money, and grey hairs. Spend wisely. Remember: complexity isn’t evil. It’s the tax we pay for power. But like any tax, you should know exactly how much you’re paying—and whether the shiny new capability really needs that third flaming torch. Closing Thoughts Agentic systems are marching toward ever broader missions, deeper memories, and wilder self-improvement loops. If you want the magic without the meltdown, measure the complexity early and often. Pick the lenses that matter for your domain, watch the numbers drift, and adjust course before the slack-line starts to sway. Because once those plates hit the pavement, no amount of post-mortem brilliance will glue them back together. Try Wordware for free . just describe your workflow in English and see it come to life.

title: CMMS Certification: What It Proves and When It's Worth It
summary: CMMS certification proves you can configure and run a maintenance system, not just use one. See which credentials are real and how to earn one.
body_text: Key Takeaways CMMS certification proves you can configure and run a maintenance system. Hiring managers screening for planner and reliability roles see it as evidence of your ability to build asset hierarchies, set PM triggers, and pull audit-ready reports without a long ramp-up. There are multiple CMMS certifications, so the right credential depends on your goal. Platform-specific badges validate one system's configuration, while vendor-neutral credentials like the CMRP cover the reliability and work-management principles applying to any system. Hands-on practice is more useful than pure reading, because exams test applied scenarios. Candidates who gain real experience clear the assessment faster than those who only review the existing body of knowledge. Certification pays off at the team level. When a manager tracks credentials and training completion in one place, knowledge transfer stops depending on the few veterans who remember how everything works. A resume that lists “CMMS experience” explains nothing. It could mean someone closed work orders on a system a manager set up for them, or that they built the entire thing. The difference usually shows up six weeks into the job, when you find out if your new planner can formulate and configure the system or only move around inside one. That gap is why certification exists, and it’s getting more expensive to ignore. Monster found that 64% of employers struggle to attract talent , and the squeeze tightens every year as experienced technicians who know these systems retire faster than new ones arrive to replace them. An authoritative credential is one of the few reliable ways to tell who can do the work before you hire them. What Is CMMS Certification? CMMS certification comprises several credentials intended for different jobs, and picking the wrong one leads to time wasted studying for an exam that won’t advance your career. Most certifications fall into one of two groups: A platform certification , which comes from a CMMS vendor and confirms you can configure its software, manage users, and build out its modules. It signifies deep knowledge of one system. A professional maintenance credential , which comes from an independent body and certifies you understand maintenance and reliability work more broadly, with CMMS administration as one piece of a wider scope. Then there’s training, which is often mistaken for certification. A course that ends with a certificate of completion just says that you sat through the material, whereas a certification shows you passed an assessment against a published standard, and that’s the delineation a hiring manager cares about. If you want to become fluent in a specific system, you need training, so start by upskilling your team to become CMMS superusers . The credentials cover the rest. Why CMMS Certification Matters If you set PM triggers on the calendar when the assets run on meter hours, you generate services that miss the wear. Some equipment gets touched too often, and the rest fails between intervals. Building an asset hierarchy with no logic to it, meanwhile, pushes the mess onto every report that pulls from it. These mistakes quietly inflate a maintenance budget, so certification is designed to test someone on these before they make the same errors on your floor. Credentials are also leverage for job candidates since they shorten the screening process for a hiring manager who can’t easily verify hands-on skills. They’re the line that separates a technician from the planner or CMMS administrator roles that pay more and carry more weight. Most people don’t move up just by waiting to be noticed. A recognized credential is how they make their case. But is it worth the money? Certification costs include fees and study hours, and the payoff is expanded capability that may lead to a significant pay bump. But avoiding a botched implementation, catching a recurring failure a few months sooner, or qualifying for a role that was previously closed to you justifies the investment several times over. Many employers cover the expenses as well, because a certified team onboards faster and leans less on the one or two people who know everything at the company. Run the numbers against where you want to be in three years to see if it’s worth it. Vendor vs. Vendor-Neutral Certifications The credential that’ll move you closer to your goals depends on which system you work in and how far you want the credential to extend beyond it. Platform certifications come from CMMS vendors themselves. You learn one system deeply, including the modules, configuration, and admin settings, then the vendor confirms you can run it. That’s sufficient for an in-house administrator whose company has committed to a platform because it maps directly to the job. The limit is in the name; it certifies you on that particular platform only, so it carries less weight the day you move to a company that operates on something else. Vendor-neutral credentials come from professional bodies and certify mastery of maintenance and reliability. They hold their value across employers and tools, which is why a hiring manager recognizes them on sight. The two worth your time are the CMRP and the CMM. The CMRP (Certified Maintenance & Reliability Professional) from SMRP carries the most weight. It’s the only credential in this space accredited by the ANSI National Accreditation Board under ISO/IEC 17024, which is highly attractive to employers who use accreditation as a baseline. Its body of knowledge runs across five pillars, but the one that concerns you most here is Work Management, which encompasses planning, scheduling, work orders, and the asset management data the whole program depends on. If you want one portable credential that says you understand maintenance broadly, this is the one to chase . The CMM (Certified Maintenance Manager) from the Association of Asset Management Professionals is the other major badge of authority. It’s built on a body of knowledge from the Uptime Elements framework and aimed at people running maintenance operations. The certification is well regarded but doesn’t hold the ANAB accreditation that the CMRP does, so take that into consideration if your employer or industry says accreditation is a must. Dimension CMRP CMM Issuing body Society for Maintenance & Reliability Professionals (SMRP) Association of Asset Management Professionals (AMP), built on Reliabilityweb's Uptime Elements Accreditation The only ANAB-accredited under ISO/IEC 17024 Recognized industry credential but not ANAB-accredited Focus Maintenance, reliability, and physical asset management across five pillars, one of which is Work Management Maintenance management across a multi-modular Strategic Maintenance Management body of knowledge Who it's for Planners, reliability engineers, and maintenance managers wanting a portable, accredited standard Maintenance managers and leads wanting a structured maintenance management credential Eligibility Open to anyone, with no degree or experience prerequisite Demonstrate competencies relevant to the body of knowledge at an intermediate level How you earn it One proctored exam, up to 2.5 hours Study the body of knowledge through the Uptime Elements Academy, then demonstrate competency Recertification Every 3 years, 50 credit hours from two or more activities Every 3 years, through AMP-approved events and conferences Cost $300 members, $470 nonmembers (USD exam fee) $399 (USD exam fee) How to Choose: Format, Cost, and Goal How you earn these certifications and what they cost differ. The CMRP is a single proctored exam that lasts up to two and a half hours and is open to anyone; no degree or minimum years of experience required (although people with a few years of work under their belt tend to find it easier). It runs $300 for SMRP members and $470 for everyone else, and it’s good for three years over 50 hours of continuing education. For the CMM, you study its body of knowledge through the Uptime Elements Academy and demonstrate mastery, then keep it current through approved events. The exam fee is $399. In comparison, vendors set the training, the test, and the price for platform certifications. They’re usually an online track, but check the specific program. You can find free and near-free “CMMS certifications” in online searches that are fine for learning a tool, but they only certify attendance. Accredited credentials cost money , but a hiring manager trusts these, so choose carefully. The Context of the Technician Path Not everyone wants a manager’s title, and the credentials account for that. The same body behind the CMRP offers the CMRT (Certified Maintenance & Reliability Technician) certification, for instance, which is accredited the same way and built around the work itself, namely, preventive and predictive tasks, troubleshooting, and corrective repairs. If you’re the one with hands on the equipment, that’s your credential. So, when does it make sense to climb from the CMRT to the CMRP? When the job starts changing around you. The CMRT proves you can execute. The CMRP extends into planning the work, setting reliability strategy, and the budgeting and analysis side of the operation. If you find yourself scheduling other people’s work, owning the PM program, or eyeing a planner or supervisor seat, start looking into the CMRP. Until then, the CMRT is enough to fit the work you’re doing, and there’s no prize for holding a credential ahead of the role. Two other credentials are worth considering as well: The CPMM (Certified Professional Maintenance Manager) from the Association for Facilities Engineering is a management credential gated behind experience and references, aimed at plant and facilities managers. If your work is more facility management with maintenance as one slice of it, the CFM (Certified Facility Manager) should be your go-to. Other CMMS certifications exist, but most are either narrower than these or not worth the effort. The ones above hold up when someone who knows the field reads your resume. How to Prepare for CMMS Certification Once you’ve picked one, the prep has the same general shape, whether it’s the CMRP, the CMRT, or a vendor exam: Determine your knowledge gaps. Pull the issuing body’s outline and honestly grade yourself in each domain. The weak spots are where to devote your study time. Study using official materials. Use the governing body’s own guides and practice exams. Third-party prep quality ranges from solid to useless, and only the official outline is guaranteed to match the test. Get hands-on practice. These exams test applied judgment over recall, so reading will only take you so far. Build asset hierarchies, set PM triggers, and pull reports in a working CMMS until it’s muscle memory. Join a study group. Local chapters and online communities trade question banks and study plans. Explaining a concept to someone else is the fastest way to find the gaps you didn’t know you had. Book the exam even if you don’t feel 100% ready. An open-ended plan gives you an excuse to push back taking the test. A date on the calendar forces you to make the last few weeks count. For a manager, prep is a tracking problem. They have to pinpoint who’s working toward what certification, who’s making time for it, who already holds which credential, etc. UpKeep Learn keeps all that information in one place. It also lets you assign the training that fits each role, monitor completion, and view every technician’s certification status next to the work they’re doing. With UpKeep Learn, you can see the team’s capability on one screen instead of reconstructing it from memory when someone hands in their two weeks’ notice. Turning Certification Into Team Capability A maintenance operation that neglects certification runs into the same problems every time: The knowledge sits with two or three veterans and lives nowhere else. New hires take months to become useful, the CMMS is used three different ways by three different people, and the same asset fails the same way every quarter because nobody reads the history. That reactive state is where more teams are headed as their most experienced people retire. Certification is one of the levers that reverses direction. It puts a documented standard under your team’s skills, shrinks onboarding, and keeps competence from leaving with a single resignation. The credential proves a person cleared the bar. Tracking it across the team in UpKeep Learn alongside the work orders and PM history tells you who’s cleared it, who’s close, and where the next gap opens before it costs you. If you’d rather view your team’s capability than guess at it, start a free UpKeep trial or book a demo . Frequently Asked Questions What is CMMS certification? Several different credentials sit under that umbrella. Some are tied to a specific CMMS platform and prove you can run that software; others are vendor-neutral maintenance credentials like the CMRP that treat CMMS work as part of a broader skill set. None is literally named “CMMS certification,” which is why search results for it look like a cluster of unrelated programs. How do you get CMMS certified? Match the credential to your goal first, then prepare using its published body of knowledge. For something like the CMRP, you apply through the issuing body, study the domains, get hands-on experience, and take a proctored exam. For a platform certification, you run the vendor’s training track and pass their test. How much does CMMS certification cost? It depends on the test. The CMRP exam is $300 for members and $470 for nonmembers, while the CMM exam fee is $399. Platform and other credentials range widely, so check the issuing body directly and budget for study materials and any membership that drops the exam fee while you’re at it. Can you get CMMS certified online or for free? You can usually study and test online, but the no-cost “certifications” you see advertised are training certificates that confirm you finished a course. They’re useful for skill development but aren’t the same as a proctored credential measured against a standard. The accredited ones charge a fee, but they’re more trustworthy to an employer. What’s the difference between CMMS training and certification? A training course hands you a completion certificate for working through the material, meaning it confirms you just finished the content. A certification puts your knowledge through a graded exam tied to an industry standard, which is what a hiring manager values. Most people end up doing both, starting with training to master a tool and then getting certified once they want to validate that knowledge. Is CMMS certification worth it? For anyone planning to stay in maintenance, usually yes. The return is greater capability over a raise though. You gain faster onboarding, fewer expensive mistakes, and access to planner and reliability roles that ask for it. While it costs money and hours, plenty of employers reimburse it, and the math works out if you’re weighing it against a whole career.

title: NEW JERSEY RESOURCES HOSTS 72nd ANNUAL MEETING
body_text: New Jersey Resources NEW JERSEY RESOURCES HOSTS 72nd ANNUAL MEETING 01/21/2025 - For Immediate Release Wall, NJ – New Jersey Resources (NYSE: NJR), today hosted its 72nd Annual Shareowners Meeting. At the virtual meeting, shareowners elected Gregory E. Aliff, Thomas C. O’Connor and Michael A. O’Sullivan to NJR’s board of directors each for a three-year term that will expire in 2028. “I appreciate our shareowners’ support for our directors and confidence in our company,” said Steve Westhoven, President and CEO of New Jersey Resources. “The expertise of Greg, Tom and Mike is an asset to our board and NJR. We have an exceptional group of directors whose integrity and vision drives our growth strategy and our commitment to delivering long-term value for our shareowners.” In other business, shareowners approved a non-binding advisory resolution on the compensation of NJR’s named executive officers and ratified the appointment of Deloitte & Touche LLP as its independent registered public accounting firm for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025. About New Jersey Resources New Jersey Resources (NYSE: NJR) is a Fortune 1000 company that, through its subsidiaries, provides safe and reliable natural gas and clean energy services, including transportation, distribution, asset management and home services. NJR is composed of five primary businesses: New Jersey Natural Gas , NJR’s principal subsidiary, operates and maintains natural gas transportation and distribution infrastructure to serve customers in New Jersey’s Monmouth, Ocean, Morris, Middlesex, Sussex and Burlington counties. Clean Energy Ventures invests in, owns and operates solar projects, providing customers with low-carbon solutions. Energy Services manages a diversified portfolio of natural gas transportation and storage assets and provides physical natural gas services and customized energy solutions to its customers across North America. Storage and Transportation serves customers from local distributors and producers to electric generators and wholesale marketers through its ownership of Leaf River and the Adelphia Gateway Pipeline, as well as our 50% equity ownership in the Steckman Ridge natural gas storage facility. Home Services provides service contracts as well as heating, central air conditioning, water heaters, standby generators, solar and other indoor and outdoor comfort products to residential homes throughout New Jersey. NJR and its over 1,300 employees are committed to helping customers save energy and money by promoting conservation and encouraging efficiency through Conserve to Preserve® and initiatives such as SAVEGREEN®. . For more information about NJR: www.njresources.com. Follow us on X.com (Twitter) @NJNaturalGas . “Like” us on facebook.com/NewJerseyNaturalGas .
